Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of stridor in infancy, typically presenting by 2–4 weeks and often worsening with feeding, supine position, or agitation; recurrent episodes at 10 months remain consistent with persistent or moderate-severe disease. Viral bronchiolitis remains highly plausible given age-related susceptibility and overlapping wheeze/stridor (especially with associated rhinorrhea, cough, or fever—though not reported); RSV and rhinovirus are frequent triggers. Tracheomalacia commonly co-occurs with laryngomalacia or vascular rings and presents with expiratory stridor/wheeze, often positional or effort-dependent. Foreign body aspiration must be considered in any infant with acute-onset or asymmetric wheeze/stridor—even without clear history—as it may present subacutely with recurrent symptoms mimicking asthma or infection. Subglottic stenosis (congenital or iatrogenic) is less common but fits recurrent stridor, especially if present since early infancy or following NICU admission/intubation. Less likely diagnoses (e.g., asthma, cystic fibrosis, vocal cord dysfunction) are excluded due to age-inappropriateness, lack of systemic features, or absence of chronic cough/failure to thrive."}

Bronchiolitis (especially RSV or rhinovirus) may cause wheeze and sometimes high-pitched upper airway noise from secretions or laryngeal edema, but typically presents acutely with viral URI symptoms—not recurrent episodic events without fever/coryza—so less likely but plausible (0.65).
